Performance Analysis on Benchmarks 1) Training Results: The comparison between SIGN and other SoTA algorithms is presented in Table I. Due to the lack of existing continuous baselines, we extend FGPrompt (a discrete SoTA method) to a continuous policy by modifying its action layer. To ensure a fair comparison, both continuous FGPrompt and SIGN are trained for the same number of steps, as illustrated in Fig. 6. On the Gibson benchmark, SIGN outperforms the continuous baseline by +6.4% in SR and +18.3% in SPL. With the augmentation of the proposed auxiliary tasks, SIGN demonstrates better training efficiency than the baseline. Theperformancegapbetweendiscreteandcontinuouspoli- cies arises from the increased task complexity. Specifically, discrete policies simplify system dynamics by updating the agent’s pose through teleportation. In contrast, continuous velocity control follows first-order integral dynamics (p˙ =v), requiring the agent to reason over continuous transitions and jointly optimize linear and angular velocities. As a result, training continuous-control policies is more challenging for RL, especially for early exploration and policy convergence. The significant performance degradation of FGPrompt when transferred from discrete to continuous actions further high- lights the challenges of continuous control in ImageNav. JSON: Name: sign_image_nav Title: Safety-aware continuous-velocity image-goal navigation for autonomous drones via reinforcement learning with auxiliary visual pretraining and depth-conditioned action correction Short Hypothesis: Augmenting an on-policy continuous-velocity image-goal navigation policy with self-supervised visual auxiliary tasks (single-step future prediction and random-shift augmentation) and a depth-conditioned collision predictor that corrects velocity commands will produce higher success rate and higher SPL on unseen indoor environments than the same continuous policy trained without these auxiliary tasks and without action correction. Related Work: Prior image-goal navigation methods fall into two broad categories: discrete-action, map-less RL and end-to-end continuous control. Discrete-action ImageNav approaches simplify exploration and control by using few high-level actions, which reduces sample complexity but relies on implicit teleportation-like pose updates and lacks fine-grained control necessary for UAVs. Continuous-control methods and imitation-based policies map images to velocity or acceleration commands, enabling precise tracking but suffering from much larger exploration spaces and sample inefficiency when trained from scratch. World-model and waypoint-planner approaches use learned or reconstructed environment representations to plan but introduce offline reconstruction, OOD generalization issues, or dependence on localization. Safety-specific designs in aerial navigation either rely on low-level controllers or reactive filters; those approaches provide obstacle avoidance but are typically decoupled from image-goal objectives and can be conservative or require additional sensors. Self-supervised auxiliary tasks (prediction, data augmentation) have been used to accelerate visual representation learning but have not been systematically combined with continuous image-goal RL for drones together with a depth-conditioned action-correction safety module. Abstract: Image-goal navigation for autonomous drones requires precise continuous control and robust visual perception while avoiding collisions in cluttered indoor environments. We propose an end-to-end framework that trains a continuous-velocity policy with on-policy reinforcement learning augmented by two self-supervised visual auxiliary tasks: single-step future latent prediction and random-shift augmentation. To enable sim-to-real transfer and ensure run-time safety, we jointly train a depth-conditioned collision predictor and apply an iterative action-correction procedure that projects unsafe continuous velocity commands toward safer alternatives. The approach eliminates reliance on external localization and explicit mapping while retaining fine-grained control. The main contributions are (1) integration of auxiliary SSL tasks into on-policy continuous-image-goal RL to accelerate representation learning and sample efficiency; (2) a depth-based collision predictor trained jointly with the policy; and (3) a lightweight action-correction mechanism that enforces obstacle avoidance at inference time. We expect improved success rates and path-efficiency in simulation benchmarks and reliable collision avoidance in real-world drone experiments without per-deployment fine-tuning. Experiments: Datasets and environments: Train on Gibson ImageNav training set (72 scenes); evaluate on Gibson test scenes (14 scenes) and cross-domain transfer to MP3D and HM3D test sets. Simulation and deployment platforms: use Habitat for RL training; use Gazebo + XTDrone + PX4 for safety and dynamic validation; perform real-world evaluation on a micro-UAV equipped with Intel RealSense D435i and onboard VIO. Policy and training regime: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with ResNet9 encoder and GRU latent, 1.6M parameters, trained from scratch for 300M environment steps with B=8 parallel environments and trajectory length L=256. Action space: continuous forward linear velocity v_lin ∈ [0,0.25] m/s and angular velocity v_ang ∈ [−15,15] °/s; stop condition v_lin<0.025 m/s and |v_ang|<1.5 °/s. Baselines: (1) discrete-action FGPrompt as published, (2) FGPrompt adapted to continuous actions (same architecture but continuous action head), (3) ZER discrete-action, (4) same continuous policy without auxiliary tasks or collision predictor (ablation). Evaluation protocol: evaluate each trained policy on 1000 episodes per difficulty mode (easy/medium/hard) per dataset; additionally evaluate 10 randomized start-goal pairs ×10 trials each in Gazebo for safety statistics and 30 real-world start-goal trials. Metrics: Success Rate (SR), Success-weighted by Path Length (SPL), average path length, collision rate per meter, collision-prediction false negative rate, action-correction invocation rate, and time-to-goal. Ablation studies: (A) remove future-prediction auxiliary task, (B) remove random-shift augmentation, (C) remove both auxiliary tasks, (D) disable collision predictor and action correction at inference, (E) compare discrete vs continuous action variants. Statistical analysis: report mean ± standard error across seeds; perform paired comparisons between SIGN and each baseline (e.g., bootstrap or paired t-test) and report p-values. Additional diagnostics: plot learning curves (reward, SR, SPL) across training steps; measure sim-to-real latency and onboard resource usage (GPU memory, CPU, inference frequency). Risk Factors and Limitations: Perception failure modes: depth sensor noise, reflective surfaces, low texture, and sunlight may produce incorrect depth vectors, causing incorrect collision probability estimates and false negatives; single-view RGB ambiguities can lead to goal-image perceptual aliasing and loop behaviors. Safety predictor limitations: the depth-conditioned collision predictor may overfit simulator depth distributions and exhibit reduced reliability under real-world depth artifacts, leading to missed collisions or excessive corrections; action-correction may induce oscillatory or lateral drift, especially during in-place rotations. Sim-to-real gaps: differences in sensor calibration, camera intrinsics, and flight dynamics (wind, latency) can degrade policy performance when transferred. Sample complexity and scalability: on-policy training of continuous policies requires large-scale environment interactions and compute; the approach may not scale to very large scene distributions without substantial training resources. Generalization limits: the method assumes target image views are reachable and reasonably similar to observations; it may fail when target views are out-of-distribution, occluded, or require long-horizon navigation through narrow, dynamic, or highly cluttered spaces. Compute and latency constraints: real-time inference and correction require sufficient onboard compute and low-latency sensors; constrained platforms may not meet these requirements, reducing safety and responsiveness.
